claims.claim: Neurotransmitters are the chemical messengers of the nervous system — chemicals released by a neuron that carry the signal across the synapse to the next cell.
The synapse (synaptic cleft) is the very small space between two neurons and an important site where communication between neurons occurs.

After the signal is delivered, excess neurotransmitters in the synapse drift away, are broken down into inactive fragments, or are reabsorbed in a process called reuptake, in which the neurotransmitter is pumped back into the neuron that released it to clear the synapse.
Dopamine is involved in mood, sleep, and learning, and is associated with attention, learning, and pleasure.
Serotonin is involved in sleep and mood and also affects hunger.
Acetylcholine is an excitatory neurotransmitter involved in muscle action and memory; it governs muscle contractions.
GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter involved in brain function and sleep, and it helps control muscle activity.
Norepinephrine is involved in alertness (OpenStax's table lists the heart, intestines, and alertness among its areas of involvement).
Some neurotransmitters make the receiving cell more active (excitatory) while others block or dampen the cell's activity (inhibitory).

Psychologists who take a biological perspective associate psychological disorders with imbalances in one or more neurotransmitter systems, and psychotropic medications treat psychiatric symptoms by restoring neurotransmitter balance.
Agonists are chemicals that mimic a neurotransmitter at the receptor site, while antagonists block or impede the normal activity of a neurotransmitter at the receptor.
Reuptake inhibitors prevent unused neurotransmitters from being transported back to the neuron, allowing them to remain active in the synaptic cleft for longer durations.

There is no one-to-one rule between a single neurotransmitter and a single behavior: each major neurotransmitter is involved in several functions, and researchers speak in broad terms about the kinds of functions associated with different neurotransmitters.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Neurotransmitter function lists vary across authoritative sources: NINDS emphasizes serotonin's roles in blood-vessel constriction, sleep, and temperature regulation, while OpenStax lists serotonin as involved in mood and sleep and Noba lists sleep, hunger, and mood.
positions: NINDS: serotonin constricts blood vessels, brings on sleep, and is involved in temperature regulation
OpenStax Psychology 2e Table 3.1: serotonin involved in mood and sleep
Noba: serotonin affects sleep, hunger, and mood
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states only the general roles supported by more than one source (serotonin: sleep, mood, and appetite/hunger) and adds the honest note that each neurotransmitter serves several functions; single-function or single-cause claims are avoided.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate — 'neurotransmitters is a foundational concept in Psychology', the 'label on a toolbox drawer' analogy, and 'a college-level explanation names the concept' — contains no factual content about neurotransmitters and was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate with a source-verified account: the working definition of neurotransmitters (attributed to OpenStax/NINDS/Noba), the synapse recap, one general role for each of the five major neurotransmitters, the reuptake mechanism, and the general drug/illness relationship (agonists, antagonists, reuptake inhibitors, imbalance/balance). All examples, scenarios, and practice questions are original to this lesson.
